seeds.hook: *Tessem*, a boy given the task of counting the names after the sickness, never got past the ninth hundred and the count is still open.
A child Hesk taught to tie a bowline in the dark, so the knot holds whether or not anyone is looking.
A tally stick notched at the height of each child in the house each year, its marks climbing toward the rafter like a boat's cut waterline.
Sea-moss streams from a dead woman's hair beneath the Leeward waves, and sailors who cut it for their nets bring bad luck to the boat.
*Tavo* laughed so hard at a fisherman's hat that he snatched it off the man's head and sailed it up past the reach of any hand.
*Hesta*, the old sailcloth stitched around a drowned body in the Leeward yards, flown above the bay for one year after the burial.
*Kattal*, the sea-anchor kite that holds a drifting boat's nose into the wind until dawn.
The drowned spread their wings to dry on the Leeward skerries before flying north, like shags at low tide, and the living are told not to look.
A stalk of kelp rises from the deepest water to the surface, and the drowned climb it at night to look for the lamps of home.
A grey heron standing still as a mooring post through the whole of the ebb, and whoever stands that long at a kelp pool is said to get the best fish.
Lemmings that march off the cliff-edge in a bad year, and Kael's net is said to be strung beneath them, though it has never once held anything.
*Tovel* — "the Trough" — is filled with split fish and salt in the last weeks of autumn, and it is visible only while the salting lasts.
*Lumma*, the male lumpfish who guards his eggs in a crevice until they hatch, is the star of men who sit by the hearth all winter while the boats go out.
Three fulmars followed a lost boat home through a fog that had no shore in it, and they still fly the same course above the north.
*Sekar*, the narwhal with its spear of tusk, is flown by the young who want to go far north and by the old who say the tusk is only a tooth that got ideas.
A kite shaped like a hunting bird, flown above the nets to frighten off the gulls, and it hangs over the Reach with its wings spread wide.
Harro dyed sailcloth red with lichen boiled in sea-water, and the red star is the vat he stirred for forty winters.
Sil, the Drowned Lantern, hung a lamp on a gull's back and sent it north to look for Aun, and the gull is still searching.

seeds.gloss: The Goat Who Would Not Come In
seeds.hook: A nanny goat refused the byre in the hungry winter and stayed out on the cliff, so Hesk keeps her at the north edge where every hearth-door can still see her.
A creature that unpicks knots and eats the loose ends is why children are taught to tie every hitch twice, and its stars are the tangles it left behind.
A dog tied to the Reel's post lifts its head at every footstep on the path, though the one it waits for has not come up the cliff in forty years.
*Ommen*, the boat that carries one lantern for every name said aloud at the harbour mouth on the night of the drowning.
She beats the sailcloth of trade boats with hail until it stiffens, and the sailors leave her their first bolt of cloth as a gift.
*Thessa*, the shuttle whose sailcloth is always unfinished in the sky because the weaver's thread ran out in the middle of a row.
The small kite flown over the bay for a child lost to the water, its tail a line of knotted cloth so the child can follow it up.
*Halun*, the puffin with a row of sand-eels crossways in its beak, is the star of the provider and of the father who comes home with his mouth full and says nothing.
A nanny goat named Mosk walked off the cliff trailing a kite-line and was hauled back up by the herd-girl, and the line still stretches across the sky.
A grey stone weight that keeps the trawl down, and that sits low in the Reach and will not rise however hard the wind pulls.
A frame of lashed driftwood where split cod hang in the wind, its rungs a row of pale stars that the Gulls count each evening.
An old man and a boy sheared the whole goat herd in one day, and their shears are a pair of crossed stars over the north cliffs.
Kael's net took a gull meant for a fallen star, and Kael let it go, so the gull now flies between the stars with a little net-mark on its wing.
Ithúna flew a tern-kite across the sound to call her husband home from the ice-grounds, and it still goes back and forth in the north when the wind is right.
A fish-trap basket with nothing in it, a cluster of gaps among the stars that marks a catch the sea kept back.
A figure with a seed-basket who scatters hail across the spring fields, and the houses bring their sacks in when they see her arm go up.
*Thorna* — "the Gaff" — hangs over the strait in high summer, when the big fish come up and must be hauled over the gunwale before they tear the net.
Children count the limpets on the rocks at the spring low tide, and Hesk is said to keep the same tally in the sky, where the number never changes.
A long eel of lightning coils through the thunderheads over the Leeward shelves and strikes the masts of boats that carry iron.
*Kessa* pulled a drowned man from the sea-ice with a bone hook, and the hook still catches the cold light of the south where the ice meets the sky.
*Mirkan*, a bowl that split in the cold, mended with pitch and sent out to the Unflown for luck.
A kite whose sail was torn in a storm and sewn back by a widow, its patch a pale square of stars that the Reach's makers point to for luck.
Orrun the Deep-Whale breathes up through the sea and spray rises to the Windward, and his spout shows as a fan of stars.
The loose end of Aun's first string is still caught on a crag in the north, where the wind keeps tugging at it.
Every winter a widow flies a black cloth kite for her husband, and the one dark patch among the stars in the north is her kite.
Ennu challenged Tavo to a kite-flying contest, Tavo tore her kite to rags, and Ennu kept the string, so the bare string is the bright line across the north.
A punch for lacing sailcloth, its ring of small stars the eyelets it leaves, and every boat-mender in the islands knows its pattern.
*Sketa* — "the Single Mitten" — has lost its partner on the ice, and it is kept lit for the child who dropped it until the child is grown.
*Sirel* — "the Quern" — is the hand-mill that turns all night at midwinter, grinding the oats for the dead, and it is the only star that never seems to stop.
The fire kept through the longest night of the year was lit from a single spark of Aun's knife, and the islanders still carry its light to their hearths.
*Sil* the Drowned Lantern sweeps her light back and forth across the southern water, searching for her brother *Aun* in every gap between the boats.
*Hatun*, the scoop a mother used to bail a sinking boat to the last, and the sky keeps it bailing the dark.

seeds.gloss: The Gull Who Lost a Word
seeds.hook: A messenger gull carrying a prayer to Vel forgot one word on the way and now flies between the Leeward and the islands trying to remember it.
*Tessal*, the kettle a voyager sets on for the one who never comes home, said never to boil in the Leeward sky.
A root torn from some warm far shore drifted in and was planted in the sand, and the wood-carvers who work it say they are carving their own homes.
*Tirun*, a boat that came home keel-up with no crew aboard and its lamps still lit underneath.
A fishwife's knife, bright at the edge where she cut her own hand, and still kept sharp by the cold stars around it.
Hesk keeps count by winding strings, and this row of stars is one star for every string she wound on the reel in the last year.
A kite that carries a small oil lamp up the line on still nights, so that boats coming in from the Leeward dark can find the harbour.
A gull of the Calm who has hung motionless for a thousand years so that no wind can reach the drowned, and sailors say its silence is the stillness that drowns the living.
A lost man asked the Gulls the way home and was told three different roads, so the stars that mark each road sit at angles to one another, and every sailor who looks at them takes a different path.
A grey hound made of falling weather that runs through the Unflown after a lost lamb, and when it barks, the rain begins somewhere in the islands.
*Tilsa* — "the Shuttle" — rises at the thaw, when the mending-thread goes back into nets that hung dry all winter.
An eider hen plucks the down from her own breast to line the nest, and the sky shows her bare and patient, which the old women say is how a mother should wait.
A cuckoo that lays her egg in another bird's nest, and the sky shows the foster bird feeding a chick that is not its own.
Two spars were tied across a narrow channel so a child who could not swim could cross to her father's boat, and the bridge now stands over the Leeward strait.
The sailmaker *Vonna* mended a torn sail during a three-day gale with her own hair for thread, and the patch is the bright smudge at the edge of the sky.

seeds.gloss: The Kite Aun Did Not Fly
seeds.hook: After he cut the string, *Aun* built a second kite to fetch the first back, but it was never flown, and it hangs unlit in the Leeward as a reminder of his regret.
A widow kept a fog-bell at the harbour mouth and rang it each night for her lost crew until the morning she stopped, and the silence she left is a dark space the sailors avoid naming.
*Sorn*, the wooden lid that keeps a hearth's warmth in while the voyagers are away, and which no one has yet lifted.
A mother flew a red kite each night from the cliff for her drowned son *Tiru* until the wind took it, and the kite now burns where it was last seen.
Ennu carved a gull from whalebone and gave it goat-hide wings so that Hesk's count could find the names of the dead by its flight.
*Mektu*, the crowberry with its black fruit on creeping hands, is the star of those who picked too far from home and came back with purple fingers and a lie.
Two lovers flew kites from opposite cliffs across the strait and tangled their lines in the middle, and the knot they made is one star they share.
A kite whose tail is tied with one knot for every winter survived, a tally Hesk keeps in the Reach where the children learn to count.
A whalebone cup passed hand to hand at weddings, so that the sky is always carrying one drink from one person to the next.
*Sulin*, the cotton-grass that burns white on the bog at dusk, is the star of wet cloth hung out to dry and of the Unflown's joke at anyone who walks toward it.
A boat's name was scraped off its hull after it was lost, so its lantern shows in the sky with no name, and the sailors say it went looking for one.
*Ennu* began a boat and a body from cloth and bone, left one rib out when the tide turned, and the gap in the frame is still visible as a dark patch.
*Tunnal*, a kite carrying a bell that rings a warning through fog for boats that cannot see the shore.
A shallow vat where brine is pressed from the catch, a white stain across the sky that the sailors use to judge the season's luck.
A skin boat shaped like a gull in flight, used by young men to row out to a girl's cliff, and its bow-star points at the rocks where she waits.
A suitor tied his string into a bowline before the house of the girl he wanted, and she untied it with her teeth and kept the cord.
A bone needle Ennu dropped on the shore after stitching the first sail, so the sky's torn places are still sewn shut from this Reach.
*Nethe*, the shag that stands on the rock with its wings spread to dry, always a little too damp, is the star for wet-weather people and for those who wait for better days.
*Kithru*, the snow buntings that come with the first snow and leave before the thaw, is the star of a first kiss in a hard year and of a promise made in the last light.
*Sarra*, the kite that cuts the lines of other kites in a Leeward contest, and whose cut string drifted off into the Upper Sea.
The net *Kael* drags through the dark is knotted from hair and has never caught a star, though the fishers of the Leeward say it has never torn either.
A flock of fog-sheep grazes low over the Leeward water, and their wool blocks the harbour mouths until Tavo's wind comes to shear it.
Lusa counted the geese going south every autumn and never missed one, and her tally is a line of bright specks that grows each year.
A boat's yard snapped in a gale and was lashed back together with kite-string, and the join still holds the shape of the sky.
A weather kite hung with a bone bell that rings when the wind turns, so the stars of its frame are said to wait for the first chime.
*Hallu*, the split cod hung on the racks, stiff as laths and white with salt, is the star of winter stores and of patience with food that has already died.
A sleeve ripped on the bird-cliffs and patched with a different cloth, kept as a sign that a mended thing can still hold wind.
A hood waxed against rain, first worn by the wife of the first kite-maker, and seen in the sky as a dark cap of stars over the Reach.
*Tiskel*, the box kite flown over the water for a drowned child, which the family sends up again each spring.
A storm-bird rides the wake of the dead down the Leeward road, sleeping on the wind and never once touching the sea.
A blind ram washed off a trade boat in a squall still swims toward the Unflown, with a length of wool-rope caught round one horn.
A pink flower that grows in a crack of the cliff in early summer, the first colour the islands see after the grey.
*Ruskel* — "the Fid" — is the splicing spike that opens a rope so new strands can go in, and it rises at the rope-making festival.
*Ketun* — "the Runner" — is the curved bone that slides the ice-road at midwinter, and it guides travellers across the frozen strait by night.
Varo sat up through three gales stitching the first storm-cloth with a bone needle in her teeth, and her needle-hand is the bright point at the kite's tail.
*Skeru*, the raven that sits on the highest stake and puts questions to the wind, is the star of old women who ask the weather too much and are answered.
A single oar that a man set down to go kiting and never came back for, which is why it still rests at the edge of the Reach.

seeds.gloss: The Comb That Beat the Last Weft
seeds.hook: *Sarven*, a weaver's beating comb that struck the final row of a sail and was set down, and it still sits in the Unflown, its teeth clean and the cloth unfinished.
A thistle of ice that blooms only in the coldest dark of the Unflown, and its seed heads are said to be the ice-lamps the lost use to find their way.
A great white tooth that Tavo the Gale lost biting a rigging-line in a fury, lodged in the Unflown, and no one who takes it can give it back.
*Ireth*, the arctic tern that flies pole to pole and back each year, is the star of the lost who turn up late, wet and unembarrassed, after the village has already grieved.
Storm-petrels nest in a crack of the north cliff and their chicks glow in the dark, so their nest shows as a cluster of soft lights.
*Kanthe*, the angelica kept green for winter, is the star of the medicine-woman's cupboard and of old quarrels smoothed over with a spoonful of seal fat.
*Hulun* — "the Crook" — is carried over the spring pastures to turn the goats uphill, and it marks the day the herds are driven to the high ground.
A nanny goat who finds the first safe ledge when the snow leaves the cliffs, and the herders follow her line up into spring.
Long brown kelp that stands up in the cold current with its hair loose, and the fisher women tie their lines to her before a storm.
*Hannel* — "the Loom Weight" — hangs from the Lamp Road to keep the sky taut, and it is said that if it ever swings, the sailcloth of the year will tear.
Sorrel leaves picked in spring and eaten against the gum-rot of the long winter, the plant that brings the blood back.
*Ruvan* scratched every gull egg of the harvest onto a bone with a hot nail, and the tally is still short by one, which the Gulls keep looking for.
*Hanor*, the stone on a line that measures how far a mast fell when it went over, and which still swings in the Leeward dark.
*Sket*, the bone hook used to haul a drowned body over the gunwale, which the sky holds out to those still in the water.
A jellyfish drifts on still water far out where no boat should go, and its bell rings faintly when a voyager is about to be lost.
A manta ray with wings of cloth-coloured skin that carries rope ends and oar-pins across the dark, delivering the gear of boats that will not come home.

seeds.gloss: The Shuttle Left in the Warp
seeds.hook: *Lotha*, a weaving shuttle abandoned mid-pass in the warp of a loom, and the cloth it crosses is the sky-dark of the Unflown itself.
When Orrun shifted under the islands he sank one arch of his ribs into the south, and the bones show as a row of pale stars that the Gulls say are still settling.
*Hulket*, the kite flown by the foolish youth of a crew to dance over the storm, at which Tavo laughs and does not tear it.
A trading crew saw a column of spray rise far south, which they knew was *Orrun* breathing beneath the sea, and they named the spot before they turned for home.
*Ulkun*, the pot every trader keeps for the crew's share, which the sky tips only at the new moon.
*Mesul*, a ferry that carries the drowned across the Leeward sea, which the islanders say touches no shore on the far side.
*Tavo* once tripped over a reef in the Leeward and scattered his own sailcloth across the sky, and the bright scraps that drifted out to sea are still there.
*Hala* cut a notch in a stick for each storm she came through, and when the stick was full she set it in the sky as a tally of survival.
*Hanthe*, the rowan with its red berries hung over doors against the sea-witch, is the star of protection and of whoever keeps the door open in a gale.
A cap tied under the chin with long ribbons, a sign of a betrothal accepted, whose streamers are a line of stars that trail toward the north.
A weaver left loose thrums at the edge of every sail so the wind would have something to hold, and the frayed ends are the stars.
Old Kesh, the kite-maker gone blind, flew her last kite by feel alone and brought it down on the stone where she was born.
Ruhk, a kite-maker who lost three fingers to frost, stitched with the stumps and never once tore a kite, and his hand is pinned above the north.
*Lesk*, born of a gust that broke in two, runs bucking across the Reach with no mother in sight, and is flown by children who want to show they can run wild.
*Tamsi* — "the Fish Kite" — is a bright red kite with a bell, flown to announce to the whole coast that the fish have come, and it rises as the first boats leave.
Herring come in autumn in a shoal so thick the boats are said to sail on it, and the nets are hung under the Lamp Road to remember the catch.
Ennu's first Sun-Kite tail frayed in a spring gale and was patched with goat-hair, and the patches still show as a row of dim stars along the road.
A mare of hail with no hooves who gallops over the drift-ice, and she is the reason the Ilvari keep a bone whistle tied to every lamp.
*Sulan*, the kite flown in mourning when no wind comes, and it hangs motionless in the deep south where no gust has reached since the first death.
Ithúna, a girl drowned off the Skarel rocks, was sent aloft on a kite her mother flew until the string parted, so the kite now hangs in the Unflown where her mother still looks for it.
Óllun sailed south to find the end of the wind, reached the Unflown, and turned his boat around, so the lantern on his mast now points toward home while his stars face the wrong way.
A sea-rope knot that Aun tied in the first days and never completed, so the Unflown has one loose loop still waiting for a hand to finish it, and that is why things go missing.
*Irel*, a ring of bone tied to a seabird's leg with a name scratched on it, which was never read by anyone, and which now circles the Unflown as a question.
A squid with eight arms wrapped around a sunken boat's lantern, holding it up to the surface for a crew that never saw it.
*Skerun*, a bone hook that Kael once cast into the southern dark, and which hangs there empty, the line having gone back to the Netter for the next fall.
*Tikar*, a child's seal-hide boot whose pair was never found on the shore, which the Unflown keeps as a pair of one, waiting for the other foot.
*Mulka*, the orca pod whose black fins stand up like sails, is flown at the launch of a new boat so the sea will see it coming and be polite.
*Kessal*, the oystercatcher with its red blade of a bill prising mussels off the rock, is the star of patient hands and of work done without thanks.
A mother asked Tavo to stop for one night so her baby could sleep, and he did, and the still patch in the north is that night.
*Hosk*, the coat that kept the sea out of its wearer until the wearer was carried out to sea inside it.

seeds.gloss: The Hare of the Dead Calm
seeds.hook: A hare runs across flat water where no wind blows, and sailors who see it know they will drift for days, and Tavo never lets it be caught.
A crab walks the sea floor counting the bones of the drowned, and Hesk, who keeps count, has not yet agreed with its total.
*Kunath*, a sleeve torn off on a gaff that still reaches out in the sky as if to take hold of another hand.
*Skelra*, the oar that snapped in the Fourteen Waters, is held up here by the woman who rowed the last stretch home on one blade.
*Oskel*, the lead on a knotted line that voyagers drop to find bottom, and which has never yet touched the bottom of Vel.
At midwinter men haul the Sun-Kite down from the road to mend it, and their rope is so stiff with frost that it rings when they pull.
*Telun* — "the Knot Belt" — carries a knot for each day of the year's labour, and one knot is untied at each festival so that the count can be seen.
*Ansu* — "the Oil Jar" — carries seal oil to the midwinter feast, and the tipping of its last drop is what the old women watch for in the sky.
A snow-spirit falls on the cliffs each winter and counts every flake against the household's stores, and its stars are the flakes it has tallied for the Reel.

seeds.gloss: The Puffin Who Lost Her Burrow
seeds.hook: A puffin blown off course in a storm could not find her way back to her burrow, so she hangs in the north, still asking the way.
Nettles are cut each spring at the edge of the field for the cloth of the house, and the stars are the stalks left standing to seed for next year.
At midsummer a couple is tied wrist to wrist with a kite-line and walks to the shore, and the line is the faint thread of stars between two lamps.
*Halenna* — "the Bride-Kite" — is flown from the bride's house to the groom's across the sound, and its tail is said to make the road the bride will walk.
A deep-water squid that carries its own light and blinks it at passing boats, which is why the fishermen say the Lamp Road is a shoal that remembers how to shine.
A mouth as wide as a rock pool opens under the reef and takes anchors and oars, and mothers keep their children's names short so it will not hear them.
*Mekle*, the wool cap a fisher's widow knitted for her son and left on a rock, which hangs above the harbour mouth in the cold months.
*Hesk* keeps count of every string, and one spool slipped from her hand during the cutting and fell south, which is why she never quite finishes her count.
A pale trunk of a tree no one on the islands grows, washed up from the far south, and it is said to have come from the Unflown.
Two fishers argued all night over when the tide would turn until it turned on its own, and they still argue, though the sea has long since settled it.
The goat chosen for the midsummer feast was marked with a red ribbon, and its horns are the two bright stars that turn toward the cooking fires.

seeds.gloss: The Race to the Standing Stone
seeds.hook: Aun won the midsummer kite race to the standing stone by cutting the other kites' lines, and the losers are still racing him up the road.
*Varo* walked backward down the rope-walk, spinning the cord as she went, and the stars are the twist of that cord that she has not yet finished.
A sea eel with a mouth like a torn net that takes hooks and lines whole, leaving the boats with nothing but frayed rope.
*Tharn*, the gutting knife left on a stone at the tide line by a man who walked out toward the Unflown and never came back.
An old cod swims with a trader's iron hook through its jaw, and wherever it turns the lines go slack and boats drift onto the Leeward rocks.
*Ilthun*, a ketch that went through the storm of Tavo with its stern stove in and still sails with its sails full.
Autumn fish were hung on poles to dry in the cold wind, and the stars lie in rows like split cod on the racks.
The Gale took a fisherman's hat on the first morning of spring and he chased it up the road, and the hat is still just out of his reach.
*Mesil* — "the Wick Shears" — cut the lamp back at the end of the dark half so the light can come up clean, and they hang in the sky for one night only.
*Ostra*, a whole sail that burned on a night of signal fires, and its ash has been drifting south ever since, glowing faintly at the edges, a bright thing gone grey.
Ennu built a kite once that stayed up with no string at all, and the constellation shows the kite alone in the dark, which the Kite-Wright sometimes says was a mistake of the wind.

seeds.gloss: The Kite Flown for the Drowned Child
seeds.hook: *Halun*, a small kite that mothers launch on the first still day after a child is taken by the sea, so the child can find the way up, and it was sent so far it lodged in the Unflown.
*Mora*, the ptarmigan that turns white in winter and brown in summer, is hung over the Reach as a joke against people who change their coats with the season.
A withy ring hung with running loops for taking gulls at the feast, left open and empty now as a warning to the greedy.
The round opening in the roof where the hearth smoke leaves, a ring of stars that the Reach's grandmothers watch to know if the house will be warm.
Puffins return to their burrows each spring, and the children count them with pebbles, and each year Hesk is asked which of them did not come back.
*Mirrek* cut the birth-cords through the midwinter nights, and the stars are the knots she tied in them before each cut.
Islanders crossing the winter strait roped together with a lamp at every belt, so no one walking in the snow could drift off alone.
A fish weir at the edge of the Leeward was built by the first family to fish there, and its stakes are still counted each season in the sky, though none can say who built it.
A school of small fish gathers beneath a sinking boat and lights its hull so the crew can find the way down, and it burns on in Vel for their sake.
*Lesk*, the iron that opens wet knots, set in the sky by a rope-mender who could not open the knot that held her son's boat.
*Lutha*, the small lamp set on a prow to show a boat the way in, of which the sky has many, and one still burning.
A skua snatches fish from gulls in mid-air, and it was set in Vel as a warning to traders who weigh their salt false.
A thing built of drift, tangled rope and broken weir-stakes walks the tideline on legs of driftwood, and any boat it touches comes home full of sand.
A stranger named *Óllun* came to the islands with blue thread that no one could dye, and the thread was wound onto the sky as a single shining line.
*Nelu*, a kite flown from one boat to another across rough water, carrying a salt token that proves the bargain.
A floe closes around boats that drift too far into the cold like a pair of jaws, and the grinding of its ice is a song the drowned hum.
After cutting the string, Aun flew a second kite from the same cliff to see whether the first was following, and it was not.
A mourning kite with a tail of black wool, flown the morning after a death so the dead can see the way up to Vel.
*Moseth*, a grey heavy ewe that leads lost lambs home through the mist by calling, is the star of whoever finds the way when no one else can see it.
A spark flew off the knife when *Aun* cut the string, fell south into the Leeward, and still burns low there, the closest thing to a warm hearth that sailors ever find.
Three bones of a dead goat were lashed together into a frame for a coracle that carried a stranded family to shore, and the frame now sails the southern sky.
One of the Gulls came too low over the Leeward carrying the names of the drowned and never returned, so its wing-tips are the faint pair of stars that islanders watch for news.
A round stone was pulled from Orrun's back by a fisher at low tide, and the house still wears it as an anchor against the wind.
She plucked the down from her own breast to line a child's cradle, and Hesk keeps her stars on the pole where the warm feathers are counted.
A limpet clings to the flat stone under the family hearth and has not moved in living memory, which is why the Ilvari say to be as hard to shift as a limpet.
A widow's soup pot fed the whole village through the hungry year, and it is said to steam still, so that no house on the islands goes without.

seeds.gloss: The Old Cod of the Deep Shelf
seeds.hook: The elders fish the great cod of the deep shelf and count its years by the rings in its scales, and its stars are the marks of the oldest year still living.

seeds.gloss: The Crow Who Stole the Tally-String
seeds.hook: A crow took a knotted count-string from the Reel's table, and though the string was spent long ago, the crow still flies the knots in its beak.
*Mesket* carried salt across the Leeward strait every month of her widowhood, and her lamp still hangs over the water where her husband's boat went down.
A grey stone was tied on a thread so it always pointed toward home, and when the thread snapped in the south the stone fell and rose again as a star that never turns.
Three gusts are tied in a knot and thrown at a boat before dawn, and any sailor who counts them wrong is taken.
*Harlu*, a low wet dog that runs the shore snapping at the heels of anyone out too late, is the star of the one who goes out in the dark to look for a lost boat.
*Skalla*, an old woman in the kelp who pulls rope and hair from drowned boats, is the star of the thing that keeps what the sea gives back and asks a hand in return.
*Haku*, the gannet that folds its wings and drops like a thrown gaff into the sea, is the star a boy takes when he dives for a girl's favour and comes up with only salt.
*Ketha*, the mending shuttle that Kael is said to borrow when he casts for fallen stars and never catches one.
A boat lit its lamp to call the lost home in a storm, and the lamp went down with it, so its light still shows just above the horizon.
An octopus creeps into fishing nets at night and unpicks the knots one by one, and the fishers say it is searching the cords for their dead men's names.
Two knitted mittens a girl made for a boy out on the water, one given in courtship and the other still waiting in the sky.
The grit-stone the Gale wets to sharpen his squalls, and the faint band of cloud beside it is the spray that never dries.
*Tekma*, the fulmar that spits oil from its gut at anyone who comes near its ledge, hangs over the Reach to warn climbers off the cliffs.
The bell on the lead goat rang through every spring kidding, and its stars are the tinkling that the mothers still listen for in their sleep.
At midsummer the Sun-Kite line is staked to a grey stone on the shore, and the stone is the one bright point that never drifts along the road.
A bank of sea-fog that comes off the water and grazes slowly along the Lamp Road, and the goats must be brought in when she bleats.
*Ennu* built the first kite-frame for his youngest sister from a split plank of wreck, and it hangs in the Spindle so that it can never blow away.
A lead weight on a cord that the Kite-Wright used to find true vertical in a new house, and that still hangs straight above the pole.
Children count the mussels on the low bed each year at the turn of the tide, and the stars are the shells they have counted and never finished.
A nanny goat stepped off the cliff-edge during a midsummer feast and kept walking on nothing, and her hoofprints are the faint stars the children count.
*Tesk*, a weaver's pin left in a seam the day the weaver went out on the water, which the Unflown keeps holding the cloth together.
*Thenu*, a shell coin laid on a boatman's palm for the crossing into the Unflown, which the boatman has not yet given back, and so no one there can leave.
*Sumel*, a pot of seal oil left uncovered beside a dying fire, which in the south is a heavy dark sheen that makes the stars around it seem to slide.
A storm-petrel so light it once pattered across the water to a boat in distress, and its footprints are a line of small stars that lead nowhere.
*Tirka*, a rope ladder that runs down from the Windward cliffs and ends in the Unflown, with no beach at its foot, and sailors say it is still being climbed by someone.
Elders keep nine embers alight each night by an old rule, and whoever lets the ninth one die must tell the house before dawn.
A salt-wight climbs the cliff wall at night and must be given bread at the top or it will pull the house-rope loose, so its stars hang over the door-hole.

seeds.gloss: The Hearth-Smoke That Climbs and Stops
seeds.hook: The smoke from a house rises straight into the Spindle and then stops at a height no one has reached, and the elders say it is waiting for someone to come home.

seeds.gloss: The Cut End of the String
seeds.hook: The piece of string Aun held when he cut the sky free is still knotted to nothing, and its short loose end is the faint line of stars that every drowned sailor is told to follow.
Hesk, who counts every string, once let a loose thread fall from the Reel and never counted it, so it hangs in the Unflown as the one thing she has not kept track of.
A coil of bladderwrack and old rope that moves in the swell like a serpent and ate the net of a boatwright who tried to pull it out of the sea.
*Ithúna* sold lamps to boats heading into the dark, and the shutter he fitted to each one is still open in the sky, showing the light he sold.
Three boats reached the edge of the known water, saw what lay past it, and turned back together, and their prows still point north, away from the Unflown.
*Vesket*, the goods boat laden with salt for the islands, whose captain is still counting the bags in the dark.
The autumn net came up so full that the boat sank a hand's width, and the crew still hauls at it, shouting over the weight.
*Ilun* — "the Tally Kite" — is flown at each new moon and drops one knot in the string for every month of the year, so that the count can be checked by the wind.
Hesk ties one knot into the Reel-cord each time the Sun-Kite turns over a moon, and the stars are the knots she has tied since Aun cut the string.
A young sea-calf who would not follow her mother down into the deep water and wandered out through the Leeward sea into the Unflown, and she still cries in a voice like a child.
A ram that fell from a sea-stack chasing a goat and now stands on the wave-tops with its horns in the cloud, a warning to climbers not to follow their animals.
Tavo laughed so hard at a sailor's joke that a gust took the sailor's cap out over the sea, and the red cap now rolls around the southern sky while Tavo claims it was never his.
A waterspout rises out of the calm and draws water from a boat the way a woman draws from a well, and it is named for Tavo's thirst.

seeds.gloss: The Knot That Would Not Loose
seeds.hook: A sailor's grandmother tied a hitch to keep her grandson's boat from drifting, and it held so well that the knot is still tied at the end of the Leeward line.
The wives of drowned men tie sea-thrift into bundles and drop them from the cliff, and the bundles are said to float north until they reach Hesk's reel.
*Torum*, a small grey man who counts the seabird eggs in the sea-caves and lets none leave, is Hesk's counter in the north, and children are told to count their fingers before bed.
Hano's dog ran the cliff path with a small kite tied to its collar so its master could find it in fog, and the dog still runs ahead of him in the sky.
A kite with no bell on its line, sent up to ask the wind a question that must not be answered in sound.
An otter carries a sail-needle in its teeth and mends the nets of fishers who drowned before finishing them, a gift Ennu is said to have given it.
A frost-woman knits cloth from sea-spray on the far side of the ice, and she wants a sailor to lend her a needle.

seeds.gloss: The Crew Who Rowed Past Their Names
seeds.hook: Eleven rowers in a long boat kept rowing after dark, and each one lost his name to the water, so only the count of oars remains in the sky.
*Tirrun*, the herring shoal that turns all at once like a cloth shaken in the wind, is the star of the net-mender's art, of many hands moving as one.
A kite flown by a courting pair, each holding one line, with the knot between them where the two strings meet at the sky's edge.
A kite that carries a lead weight on its tail to measure how high the wind stands, its string a plumb line dropped from the pole.
A waterspout that spins like a woman drawing up a net, and dancers on the islands copy her turns to ask the Unflown for a safe return.

seeds.gloss: The Ship in Its Own Wake
seeds.hook: A voyager's boat sailed so far south that it came around the pole and met its own wake, so the pair of stars that mark the boat and its trail are always chasing each other.
Sil, the Drowned Lantern, walks the Unflown each season carrying a single lamp, and the one star that shifts its place each year is her light searching for Aun.
Two sisters in a sinking boat traded places so the younger could reach the rope first, and their two lights now rise and set together in the south.
A grey hound with bell-teeth runs the ebb and hunts boats that come in late, and it is said to be a hound Aun once left behind.
A puffin carries a coin of salt-weight in its beak between the islands and the far trading ports, and it returns only when the price is fair.
At midsummer shearing the sky-ewe lies with her fleece pulled off and the wool hung along the Lamp Road to dry, so the summer sky smells of lanolin.
*Tarun* — "the Oilskin" — is the coat of those who go out for the last boats of autumn, and it hangs on the sky over the harbour until every boat is in.

seeds.gloss: The Kite Flown for a Drowned Child
seeds.hook: *Minsa* — "the Child's Kite" — is flown every spring with its string left long on purpose, so the drowned child can find her way home if the wind is kind.
*Thisa*, the sea-thrift that flowers in a crack of the cliff where nothing should grow, is the star of the stubborn and of children born on the ledge.
Mesket's son walked into fog after a lost kite and was led home by its tail brushing his cheek, and the tail is left hanging in the sky.
Tavo the Gale blew a fisherman's hat off his head and laughed so hard he dropped it three times, and the hat is a small star that never lands.
*Ommar* — "the Awl" — is drawn out in autumn when the women sew the winter sails, and it is said to pierce the first cloud of the season.
*Lamet* — "the Name-Kite" — is flown at midsummer for an elder who has gone aloft, and it carries the elder's name on a strip of cloth up the Lamp Road.
*Hani* — "the Wool-Cutter" — cut the spring fleece so fast that her blade threw sparks, and the sparks are the stars still falling off the goats' backs.
A plain white kite raised at a wedding so the wind can bless the couple, its tail trailing down toward the bride's new house.
*Ruvem*, who sits on boats and freezes the rope, sail and oar until they are stiff as bone, is flown by widows and by all who keep a cold house.
Women lowered baskets on long cords down the sea-cliffs each spring for gulls' eggs, and the cords now hang in the north as a row of faint stars.
*Kovar*, a grey mare who gallops over the sea throwing ice, whose hooves are the lost stones of the shore, is flown on the first hard day of winter.
Mesket read coming squalls in the way gulls turned over the bay, and she is the watcher whose eyes face the cold north.
The clay pot of lamp-fat set by the door, a small warm knot of stars that the Reach's households light first when the nights grow long.
*Oreth* waited through the whole summer for the sun to dry the brine in her shallow pans, and her pans are the bright square stars along the shore of the road.
A keeper sat by the smokehouse fire every night of winter, and the small light at the door is her, still keeping the smoke going.
*Tamun* cut her dead husband's shawl into a sail for the boat that will fetch him back from the Upper Sea, and she is still stitching it.
A thin grey climber that goes up the sea-cliffs in the dark months and taps at the shutters, and families leave a bowl of goat's milk on the step.
A slender birch the islanders plant for a newborn, which grows as the child grows, and its pale trunk rises beside the Lamp Road each spring.
*Mirrak* — "the Water Bag" — is a goatskin bottle slung on the drive to summer pasture, and its stitching is said to show when the road is long.
*Ivru* — "the Hood" — is sewn for a newborn in early spring, and it is the first garment the child wears on the road outside the house.
A grey seal who lifts her head at every burial on the shore and sings one low note that makes the mourners stop talking.
*Sekul* — "the Bailer" — is the gourd scoop that empties the boats after the spring rains, and it rises when the thaw-floods come down the valleys.
*Vanu*, the great skua that robs the gulls of their fish low over the water, is the star of borrowed things that are never given back and of the Gulls' long complaint.
*Sirav*, the eider hen who plucks her own breast to line a nest not yet built, rises as a sign of a woman who gives her warmth before she is asked.
*Remu*, the grey seal whose song under the ice is heard by drowned sailors' widows, is the star of those who listen at night for a sound that never comes.
A carding comb of driftwood teeth whose seven gaps are the gusts that tease the northern pass into wool.
*Vular*, the bladderwrack whose air-bladders rattle when the wave goes over, is the star that tells fishers the tide has turned by sound alone.
*Lumma*, the male lumpfish who guards his eggs in a crevice until they hatch, is the star of men who sit by the hearth all winter while the boats go out.
A thistle grows on the outermost skerry with its roots in salt, and it is said to be the last plant that holds a lost boat to the shore.
Each spring a nanny goat lost from a wrecked boat climbs out of the sea onto the nearest cliff, though no one has ever found her hut.
A ray sleeps beneath the hulls in the cold months, warming the keel so the boat does not freeze, and it is paid for with the first catch.
*Sathrun*, the long-tailed kite a wife flies each dusk for a ferry that is not yet home.
Sea-moss streams from a dead woman's hair beneath the Leeward waves, and sailors who cut it for their nets bring bad luck to the boat.
*Tavo* laughed so hard at a fisherman's hat that he snatched it off the man's head and sailed it up past the reach of any hand.
Three fulmars followed a lost boat home through a fog that had no shore in it, and they still fly the same course above the north.
*Sekar*, the narwhal with its spear of tusk, is flown by the young who want to go far north and by the old who say the tusk is only a tooth that got ideas.
A kite shaped like a hunting bird, flown above the nets to frighten off the gulls, and it hangs over the Reach with its wings spread wide.
Harro dyed sailcloth red with lichen boiled in sea-water, and the red star is the vat he stirred for forty winters.
Sil, the Drowned Lantern, hung a lamp on a gull's back and sent it north to look for Aun, and the gull is still searching.
The small kite flown over the bay for a child lost to the water, its tail a line of knotted cloth so the child can follow it up.
*Halun*, the puffin with a row of sand-eels crossways in its beak, is the star of the provider and of the father who comes home with his mouth full and says nothing.
A nanny goat named Mosk walked off the cliff trailing a kite-line and was hauled back up by the herd-girl, and the line still stretches across the sky.
A grey stone weight that keeps the trawl down, and that sits low in the Reach and will not rise however hard the wind pulls.
A frame of lashed driftwood where split cod hang in the wind, its rungs a row of pale stars that the Gulls count each evening.
An old man and a boy sheared the whole goat herd in one day, and their shears are a pair of crossed stars over the north cliffs.
Kael's net took a gull meant for a fallen star, and Kael let it go, so the gull now flies between the stars with a little net-mark on its wing.
A hollow reed the wind plays through in the Unflown, and the Ilvari hear its note at a funeral and say it is the voice of someone who died without a song.
Kenna's goat walked off the cliff path chasing a gull, fell all the way down to the sea, and was flung into the Unflown, where its horned outline is the only star-shape that still looks surprised.
A kelp-woman who married a fisherman on a hot calm day and grew her stalk up through the sky after he was lost, and her long brown fronds still sway in the Unflown.
Ithúna flew a tern-kite across the sound to call her husband home from the ice-grounds, and it still goes back and forth in the north when the wind is right.
A fish-trap basket with nothing in it, a cluster of gaps among the stars that marks a catch the sea kept back.
A kite whose sail was torn in a storm and sewn back by a widow, its patch a pale square of stars that the Reach's makers point to for luck.
Orrun the Deep-Whale breathes up through the sea and spray rises to the Windward, and his spout shows as a fan of stars.
The loose end of Aun's first string is still caught on a crag in the north, where the wind keeps tugging at it.
Every winter a widow flies a black cloth kite for her husband, and the one dark patch among the stars in the north is her kite.
Ennu challenged Tavo to a kite-flying contest, Tavo tore her kite to rags, and Ennu kept the string, so the bare string is the bright line across the north.
A punch for lacing sailcloth, its ring of small stars the eyelets it leaves, and every boat-mender in the islands knows its pattern.
A fishwife's knife, bright at the edge where she cut her own hand, and still kept sharp by the cold stars around it.
The stub of cut string that trails from the pole marks where the sky first came loose, and the elders touch it for luck before they count.
A wooden bowl of tallow and sinew in which cracked kite-ribs were soaked, kept by the house that lost its youngest to the sea.
A woollen mitten that has lost its pair, which the Spindle keeps hung on a nail because someone is always looking for the other one.
*Hesta*, the old sailcloth stitched around a drowned body in the Leeward yards, flown above the bay for one year after the burial.
*Kattal*, the sea-anchor kite that holds a drifting boat's nose into the wind until dawn.
The drowned spread their wings to dry on the Leeward skerries before flying north, like shags at low tide, and the living are told not to look.
A stalk of kelp rises from the deepest water to the surface, and the drowned climb it at night to look for the lamps of home.
*Ommen*, the boat that carries one lantern for every name said aloud at the harbour mouth on the night of the drowning.
She beats the sailcloth of trade boats with hail until it stiffens, and the sailors leave her their first bolt of cloth as a gift.
*Thessa*, the shuttle whose sailcloth is always unfinished in the sky because the weaver's thread ran out in the middle of a row.
A long eel of lightning coils through the thunderheads over the Leeward shelves and strikes the masts of boats that carry iron.
*Kessa* pulled a drowned man from the sea-ice with a bone hook, and the hook still catches the cold light of the south where the ice meets the sky.
*Mirkan*, a bowl that split in the cold, mended with pitch and sent out to the Unflown for luck.
*Sil* the Drowned Lantern sweeps her light back and forth across the southern water, searching for her brother *Aun* in every gap between the boats.
*Hatun*, the scoop a mother used to bail a sinking boat to the last, and the sky keeps it bailing the dark.
*Ránu* — "the Ribbon" — is the long trailing ribbon behind the Sun-Kite, and it is said to reach furthest at midsummer, when the kite is flown highest.
Mesket baked the harvest bread too hot and burned the first loaf black, and the Gulls carried it up the road as a dark star that nobody will eat.
Aun flew a second kite along the road after the cut, looking for the place where the string had gone, and it has not yet come down.
Hesk keeps count by winding strings, and this row of stars is one star for every string she wound on the reel in the last year.
A kite that carries a small oil lamp up the line on still nights, so that boats coming in from the Leeward dark can find the harbour.
Ennu carved a gull from whalebone and gave it goat-hide wings so that Hesk's count could find the names of the dead by its flight.
A kite with two long tails that a widow flies alone on the first calm day after mourning, tails pulling in different directions.
The warp of *Rahu*'s sailcloth loom, four hundred threads strung across the north, is still being woven by someone who is not yet born.
*Ithúna* notched a bone each time the water turned, and her bone rope now runs the length of the Spindle.
*Mektu*, the crowberry with its black fruit on creeping hands, is the star of those who picked too far from home and came back with purple fingers and a lie.
Two lovers flew kites from opposite cliffs across the strait and tangled their lines in the middle, and the knot they made is one star they share.
A kite whose tail is tied with one knot for every winter survived, a tally Hesk keeps in the Reach where the children learn to count.
*Surel* — "the Walker" — is carried across the ice before the travellers, its line marking the safe path, and it is put down when the far shore is reached.
A man hangs over the sea-cliff on a rope in early summer, cutting eggs from the guillemot ledges, and the knot he ties is one no one has ever cut.
Geese that leave in a wedge each autumn for the warm water past the Leeward Reach, and the wedge is said to point the way a drowned boat should have come home.
A whalebone cup passed hand to hand at weddings, so that the sky is always carrying one drink from one person to the next.
*Sulin*, the cotton-grass that burns white on the bog at dusk, is the star of wet cloth hung out to dry and of the Unflown's joke at anyone who walks toward it.
A shallow vat where brine is pressed from the catch, a white stain across the sky that the sailors use to judge the season's luck.
*Olun* — "the Needle-Mother" — sewed the first sailcloth on the midwinter, and her stitches stayed up in the sky when the cloth below wore through.
Tavo tore a curved piece from the Sun-Kite's edge in a spring gale, and the bent moon is the cloth he dropped, which the Sun-Kite is still missing.
In spring the sea breaks the ice and a boat pushes through the floes with one long oar, a pale line of stars that marks where the ice gave way.

seeds.gloss: The Gull Who Lost a Word
seeds.hook: A messenger gull carrying a prayer to Vel forgot one word on the way and now flies between the Leeward and the islands trying to remember it.
*Tessal*, the kettle a voyager sets on for the one who never comes home, said never to boil in the Leeward sky.
A root torn from some warm far shore drifted in and was planted in the sand, and the wood-carvers who work it say they are carving their own homes.
A skin boat shaped like a gull in flight, used by young men to row out to a girl's cliff, and its bow-star points at the rocks where she waits.
A suitor tied his string into a bowline before the house of the girl he wanted, and she untied it with her teeth and kept the cord.
A bone needle Ennu dropped on the shore after stitching the first sail, so the sky's torn places are still sewn shut from this Reach.
*Kestu*, lowered on a line down the cliff to take gull eggs in early summer, felt the rope go slack and was never hauled up, so she hangs on the road still.
*Kessa* — "the Cut Kite" — had its string bitten through by a gull on the longest day, and it drifts along the Lamp Road still, looking for the hand that let it go.
A stoat that turns white at the first frost and runs the Lamp Road all winter, visible only by the black tip of its tail, so children are told to keep quiet when they see it.
*Kesmar*, a wooden wedge driven into a split log to open it, which stuck fast and was left, and it is said to be splitting something far south that will never fall apart.
Ennu began a gull from cloth and bone for a grieving widow, stopped when the widow died, and left the bird with one wing unstitched, which the stars still show as a gap.

seeds.gloss: The Float Cut From Its Net
seeds.hook: *Ilmat*, a cork float cut loose from a net in a squall, which bobs in the Unflown far from any water and marks the place where a catch was lost.
*Nethe*, the shag that stands on the rock with its wings spread to dry, always a little too damp, is the star for wet-weather people and for those who wait for better days.
*Kithru*, the snow buntings that come with the first snow and leave before the thaw, is the star of a first kiss in a hard year and of a promise made in the last light.
Lusa counted the geese going south every autumn and never missed one, and her tally is a line of bright specks that grows each year.
White seed-heads of bog cotton picked in winter to stuff pillows, the soft thing the poor sleep on.
Cod split and hung on racks in the frost, a row of stiff fish turning slowly as the wind works the salt into them.
*Skelra* — "the Split Oar" — is the boat-oar that cracked on the midsummer crossing and was lashed with wet hide, and it still rows the Lamp Road.
A bone-thin thing weaves at night and undoes whatever the day has finished, so the weavers leave the last thread loose for it and its stars are the threads it has taken.
The plain square kite with no tail that a child flies before learning to read the wind, and so it is the first kite of every household.
*Mesket* kept her fire lit for nineteen winters after her husband's boat failed to come home, and each night she warmed one stone and set it by the empty place.
A boat's yard snapped in a gale and was lashed back together with kite-string, and the join still holds the shape of the sky.
A weather kite hung with a bone bell that rings when the wind turns, so the stars of its frame are said to wait for the first chime.
*Hallu*, the split cod hung on the racks, stiff as laths and white with salt, is the star of winter stores and of patience with food that has already died.
*Tirun*, a boat that came home keel-up with no crew aboard and its lamps still lit underneath.
Two spars were tied across a narrow channel so a child who could not swim could cross to her father's boat, and the bridge now stands over the Leeward strait.
The sailmaker *Vonna* mended a torn sail during a three-day gale with her own hair for thread, and the patch is the bright smudge at the edge of the sky.
A sleeve ripped on the bird-cliffs and patched with a different cloth, kept as a sign that a mended thing can still hold wind.
A hood waxed against rain, first worn by the wife of the first kite-maker, and seen in the sky as a dark cap of stars over the Reach.
Varo sat up through three gales stitching the first storm-cloth with a bone needle in her teeth, and her needle-hand is the bright point at the kite's tail.
A tubular bone sheath that holds the knitting needles of a household, its open mouth turned toward the north where the Reel winds.

seeds.gloss: The Water Jar with a Lid
seeds.hook: A covered clay jar that holds the house's fresh water through the dry months, its lid tied down with rope so the Gulls cannot get in.
A rowan tree grows by the door of every house and keeps the wind-wights out, and its red berries are the stars that stay lit through the longest night.
*Skeru*, the raven that sits on the highest stake and puts questions to the wind, is the star of old women who ask the weather too much and are answered.
A single oar that a man set down to go kiting and never came back for, which is why it still rests at the edge of the Reach.
*Ireth*, the arctic tern that flies pole to pole and back each year, is the star of the lost who turn up late, wet and unembarrassed, after the village has already grieved.
*Kenut*, a wooden bailer whose bottom rotted through, used by someone who kept trying to empty a boat that would not stop filling, and it still scoops the south.
*Nasmi*, a length of rope untwisted back into its separate fibres, the way the dead are said to come apart in the Unflown, each strand going its own way.
A crab that walks the underside of the Unflown, scraping at the edges of the sky for things that fell out of Vel, and it never gives back what it finds.

seeds.gloss: The Kite Aun Did Not Fly
seeds.hook: After he cut the string, *Aun* built a second kite to fetch the first back, but it was never flown, and it hangs unlit in the Leeward as a reminder of his regret.
A widow kept a fog-bell at the harbour mouth and rang it each night for her lost crew until the morning she stopped, and the silence she left is a dark space the sailors avoid naming.
*Sorn*, the wooden lid that keeps a hearth's warmth in while the voyagers are away, and which no one has yet lifted.
Storm-petrels nest in a crack of the north cliff and their chicks glow in the dark, so their nest shows as a cluster of soft lights.
*Kanthe*, the angelica kept green for winter, is the star of the medicine-woman's cupboard and of old quarrels smoothed over with a spoonful of seal fat.
*Hanthe*, the rowan with its red berries hung over doors against the sea-witch, is the star of protection and of whoever keeps the door open in a gale.
A mother flew a red kite each night from the cliff for her drowned son *Tiru* until the wind took it, and the kite now burns where it was last seen.
A boat's name was scraped off its hull after it was lost, so its lantern shows in the sky with no name, and the sailors say it went looking for one.
*Ennu* began a boat and a body from cloth and bone, left one rib out when the tide turned, and the gap in the frame is still visible as a dark patch.
A broody hen who sits on the lightning eggs, and when she shifts her weight the spring storms come round the islands.
*Ulsa* — "the Frame" — is the wooden rack where the fish hang to dry in spring, and its shape is said to be the first map of the islands.
*Ketha* — "the Pot Hook" — rises at the first frost, when the stew-pots come in from the yard and are hung over the fire for the winter.
*Halan* — "the Ferry Sail" — is a small square sail raised for the first crossing of spring, and it is flown low over the sound until the boat has landed.
*Kesun* — "the Whetstone" — wears a little thinner every year and rises at the turn of the year, when the knives go out for the seal-hunt.
A tern that rides the gale farther than any other bird, and Tavo is said to laugh when it is caught and carried off the road.
Hesk's two hands, held open at the pole, carry the count of every knot she has wound into the string since Aun cut it.
A wooden foot-form around which the boots of the drowned were shaped so that they could walk the Upper Sea without slipping.

seeds.gloss: The Old Gannet of the Stacks
seeds.hook: She has nested on the same sea-stack longer than any house has stood, and the elders say she counts the stacks each dawn so none goes missing.
*Tunnal*, a kite carrying a bell that rings a warning through fog for boats that cannot see the shore.
*Sarra*, the kite that cuts the lines of other kites in a Leeward contest, and whose cut string drifted off into the Upper Sea.
The net *Kael* drags through the dark is knotted from hair and has never caught a star, though the fishers of the Leeward say it has never torn either.
